R07-A-01: Discussions of the unreliable narrator tend to treat it as a game of detection. A narrator tells us one thing, the novel quietly lets us see another, and the pleasure lies in catching the gap: the jealous husband who insists he is perfectly calm, the child who reports adult quarrels without understanding them. Critics have catalogued the signals by which such narrators give themselves away, the protest that is too insistent, the detail that contradicts a claim made a page earlier, and readers have learned to watch for them. On this account the device is a kind of puzzle, and a reader who has spotted the discrepancy has finished the work the book asked of her. The narrator was wrong; the reader, standing above him, is right. This picture is not false, but it is thin. It assumes that behind every unreliable account there stands a reliable one, which the attentive reader reconstructs and then keeps. Yet the clues by which we detect a narrator's distortions are supplied by the same narrator. We infer that the husband is jealous from what he notices, what he repeats, what he cannot stop describing; we have no other witness. The true story we assemble is therefore itself an interpretation, built from the materials of the account we have decided to distrust, and we hold it with a confidence that the novel has done nothing to guarantee. What the best uses of the device achieve, then, is not the replacement of a bad narrator by a good reader but a change in how the reader regards narration as such. Having learned to read one voice against itself, we begin to notice how much we ordinarily grant to voices that give no sign of strain: the calm third-person narrator of a realist novel, the memoirist, the friend recounting a quarrel. None of them is lying, perhaps, but all of them select, arrange and omit. The difference is one of degree rather than kind; the narrator we call reliable is simply one whose selections we have not thought to question. The unreliable narrator makes visible a condition that reliable narration merely conceals. It must be admitted that not every novel built on an untrustworthy teller rises to this. Some use the device as a trapdoor, a revelation held back for the final chapters that turns everything before it into misdirection. Such books can be thrilling once. On a second reading, however, they tend to go flat, because the only question they posed has been answered. The novels that survive rereading are those in which the distrust never quite settles, in which the reader, having caught the narrator out, is left wondering what she herself has failed to see.
R07-A-02: A persistent habit of literary talk treats the short story as a smaller novel: the same materials of character, setting and incident, simply supplied in lesser quantities. On this view the story is where writers practise before attempting the larger form, and a collection of stories is a kind of portfolio of novels not yet written. The habit is reinforced by publishers, who have long regarded collections as harder to sell, and by critics who praise a story for being 'as rich as a novel', as though richness of that kind were the measure of success. Prizes and anthologies have sometimes followed suit, treating a writer's stories as preparation and the first novel as the real debut. The comparison misunderstands where a short story does its work. A novel accumulates; it earns its effects through duration, letting the reader live alongside its people for enough days that change in them can be felt as change. A story has no such time to spend. What it has instead is selection, and selection pressed hard enough becomes a kind of meaning in itself. When a story shows a woman packing a suitcase, pausing over a single photograph and putting it back in the drawer, the eleven years of marriage that the story never describes are present precisely because they are withheld. The reader does not receive them; she supplies them, and the supplying is the experience. This is why expanding a fine story so rarely improves it. Give the woman a history, a sister to confide in, a chapter on the courtship, and the photograph becomes one detail among many rather than the point on which everything turns. The gaps that had been doing the work are filled with information, and information, however well written, is less charged than implication. The reader who had been supplying the marriage is now simply told about it, and being told is a lesser kind of participation. The story's brevity was not a limitation it laboured under but the condition of its force. None of this means that stories and novels never meet. Some writers have plainly used stories as sketches, and more than one long novel began as a few pages its author could not leave alone. Nor is brevity a virtue in itself; a weak story can hide behind its shortness, gesturing at depths it has not earned. The claim is narrower: that when a story succeeds on its own terms, it succeeds by a method the novel mostly cannot use, and that judging it by the novel's standards will reliably mistake its strengths for omissions.
R07-A-03: Among serious readers there is a settled suspicion of the happy ending. A novel that closes with a wedding, a reconciliation or a recovered fortune is assumed to have flinched at the last moment, to have given its audience what it wanted rather than what its story required. An ending in death, separation or failure, by contrast, is credited with courage. The assumption behind the contrast is rarely stated but easy to reconstruct: life does not resolve itself neatly, so a book that resolves neatly must be telling a comforting lie. The suspicion is old enough to have become a reflex, and few readers who share it could say where they acquired it. There is something to this, since the history of popular fiction is crowded with endings that arrive from outside the story, the unexpected legacy, the villain who repents in a paragraph, the rival who conveniently dies, and readers are right to feel cheated by them. Such endings resemble a rescue by a passing stranger: welcome, perhaps, but unconnected with anything the characters have done. But the fault in such endings is not their happiness. It is that nothing in the preceding chapters made them necessary. A catastrophe imposed in the same way, a heroine killed by a runaway carriage because the author wanted the book to feel weighty, is no less arbitrary and, being arbitrary, no more truthful. The prejudice persists, I think, because it confuses two things that endings do. Every ending closes; it marks the point after which the story will not be told. Some endings also console; they leave the reader reassured about the world the book has shown. Closure is a formal necessity, since a story must stop somewhere, while consolation is a choice. The suspicious reader notices that happy endings console, objects to the consolation, and then mistakes the objection for an argument against closure itself, as though the honest book would be the one that refused to finish. Yet an unhappy ending closes just as firmly; it simply closes on a different note, and that note can be just as comfortably familiar to readers who have learned to expect gloom from serious fiction. The better test, then, is an internal one: an ending is honest when it is the place towards which the book's own pressures have been carrying it, so that a reader looking back can see how the earlier pages prepared it, whether that place is a marriage or a grave. By this test some happy endings are among the hardest-won things in fiction, and some tragic ones are merely fashionable. The question to ask of an ending is not whether it pleases but whether it follows.
R07-A-04: The line between literary and genre fiction is usually drawn in terms of freedom. The literary novel, it is said, invents its own shape, while the crime novel, the romance and the tale of space travel arrive with their shapes already supplied: a body in the first chapter, an obstacle between the lovers, a voyage, a crisis and a return. To write in a genre is, on this account, to fill in a form someone else designed, and the best a genre writer can hope for is to fill it in with unusual skill. Critics who accept this account tend to praise a crime novel by saying that it rises above its genre, as though the genre were something to be escaped. The account has the logic of constraint backwards. Nobody thinks a sonnet a lesser poem because its length and rhyme scheme were fixed before the poet began. We understand that the fixed form is what makes certain effects possible: a turn in the ninth line registers as a turn only because the reader knows where turns are expected. Genre conventions work in much the same way. A reader of detective stories knows that the culprit must be among the people introduced, that the clues must be fair, that a solution will come. These expectations are not a cage around the writer but an instrument she can play, and the slightest departure from them, a detective who is wrong, a solution that satisfies the law but not the reader, is felt with a precision no unconventional novel can command, because the unconventional novel has no settled expectation to depart from. This is also why devoted readers of a genre are often its most exacting critics. Having read a hundred novels built on the same frame, they are alert to the smallest variation in it, much as a chess player who knows an opening thoroughly notices a single unusual move that a novice would pass over. Such readers can tell at once whether a twist is earned or merely borrowed, and they are rarely generous to a writer who mistakes one for the other. Their pleasure is not the passive pleasure of repetition but the active one of comparison. None of this rescues every genre book. Conventions harden into formula when a writer treats them as a checklist to be completed rather than an expectation to be worked against, and a great deal of genre fiction is written in exactly this way. But the same is true of literary fiction, which has its own conventions, the quiet revelation in the final paragraph, the fractured chronology, the unnamed narrator, and its own writers who complete them dutifully. The useful distinction is not between books that have conventions and books that lack them, since none lack them, but between books that do something with their conventions and books that merely obey them.
R07-A-05: The commonest objection to free verse is that it is merely prose with the margins moved. Take away the rhyme and the regular metre, the objection runs, and nothing distinguishes a poem from a paragraph except the typographer's decision to stop each line short of the edge of the page. If that decision is arbitrary, the poem is a pretence; if it is not, the objector would like to know what principle governs it, and a vague appeal to the poet's ear or instinct will not satisfy him. The question deserves a better answer than poets usually give it, and the principle, where there is one, is that the line is a unit of attention. A reader pauses, however slightly, at the end of a line, and in that pause whatever the line has said is briefly complete. A sentence broken across two lines is therefore read twice: once as the line presents it and once as the sentence finally does. Consider a line that ends 'she said she would not leave', followed by one that begins 'the house until the rain had stopped'. For the length of the pause the woman refuses to leave at all; the next line shrinks the refusal to a matter of weather. Neither reading cancels the other; the poem holds the larger refusal and the smaller one together, and prose, which delivers its sentences whole, cannot easily do this. Line breaks also govern pace, since a poem made of short lines slows the reader, weighting each word with a pause, while long lines carry her forward faster than the sense alone would. Where metre once supplied a regular beat against which a poet could set the natural stresses of speech, the free verse poet works with the silence at the ends of lines, which is a cruder instrument than metre but not a negligible one, and which has the compensating advantage that it can be varied from line to line without breaking any rule. None of this shows that the objection is always wrong. A good deal of what is published as free verse is broken into lines for no reason a reader could recover, and in such cases the objection is simply correct: the lines could be run together without loss. A fair test is exactly that: set the poem out as prose, read it again, and ask what has gone. If nothing is lost, if no meaning that the breaks created has vanished and no pace has been flattened, then the breaks were decoration. What the test cannot do is condemn the form as such, since in the poems that pass it the breaks turn out to have been doing work that the prose version cannot preserve.
R07-A-06: Few critical preferences are as widely shared as the preference for round characters over flat ones. A round character, in the usual formulation, has an inner life complex enough that it can change, contradict itself and still remain recognisable; a flat character is built around a single trait and can be summed up in a sentence. The first is praised as lifelike, the second tolerated as a convenience, useful for filling a drawing room or delivering a message but not to be mistaken for the real achievement of fiction. Yet the preference rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny: that the novel's central business is the representation of individual inner life. That has been the business of one powerful tradition, but it is not the only thing novels do. Many of the novels readers return to are as much about a society as about a self, and a society is felt in fiction partly through the people who never change: the aunt who has said the same thing at every family dinner for thirty years, the official for whom every request is a breach of procedure. Their fixity is not a failure of imagination. It is how the novel registers the pressure of a world that does not bend, against which its few changing figures can be measured. Flat characters also carry much of fiction's comedy, which depends on repetition. A man who responds to every misfortune by consulting the same almanac is funny the third time precisely because he could not have done otherwise. Deepen him, give him a moment of doubt about the almanac, and the joke dissolves into pathos; this may be a gain, but it is a different book. There is, too, a case that flatness is closer to ordinary experience than critics allow. Most of the people we know, we know only by a few habits and phrases, and a novel that rendered every acquaintance in the round would misrepresent how other people actually appear to us, however much it flattered our sense of their depth. This is not to invert the hierarchy. A novel peopled entirely by flat characters would be a cartoon, and the moment when a figure we had thought simple reveals unexpected depth remains one of fiction's great effects, though it depends on our having first taken him as simple. The point is that flat and round are not grades of achievement but different tools, suited to different tasks, and a criticism that rewards only one of them will misread every novel in which both are at work.
R07-A-07: The word from which the essay takes its name once meant an attempt or a trial, the act of testing something by weighing it, and the form has never quite outgrown that sense. An essay, in its original spirit, is not the report of a conclusion already reached but the record of a mind trying a thought to see whether it will bear weight. It may change direction halfway through, concede more than it intended, or end with a question sharper than the one it started with. These are not lapses. They are the form doing what it was invented to do, and the reader of such an essay is permitted to overhear a mind in conversation with itself rather than merely to receive the outcome of that conversation. It is worth noticing how far the essay most people now encounter has moved from this. The essay that is taught in schools and demanded in universities opens with a thesis, marshals evidence in its favour, dispatches objections and restates the thesis at the close. It is, in effect, a miniature treatise, and its virtues are those of the treatise: clarity of claim, economy of proof, a structure the reader can grasp in advance. These are real virtues, and there are good reasons to teach them, not least that a writer who cannot state a claim plainly is in no position to test it. But the result is that a generation of writers has learned to regard any movement of thought within a piece of writing as a defect of planning, something to be removed in revision so that the finished text looks as though its conclusion had been visible from the first sentence. What is lost is not merely a style. The provisional essay offers something the treatise structurally cannot: a view of how a conclusion is reached, including the paths that were tried and abandoned. A reader who watches a writer test an idea against an example, find that it fails, and adjust it, learns not only where the writer arrived but how much the arrival cost and what it excluded. She is reminded, too, that the conclusion was reached by someone who could have been wrong and who knows it. The treatise presents its conclusion as if it were the only place the evidence could lead; the essay, by showing the alternatives it passed through, leaves the reader better placed to disagree. In this sense its apparent modesty is a form of candour about the limits of its own claims. The same candour explains the essayist's much criticised first person. The 'I' of the essay is often taken for self-display, and sometimes it is exactly that. More often it marks the scope of a claim: this is how the matter looks from here, to someone with this experience, and the reader is invited to test it against her own. The impersonal voice of the treatise, by contrast, claims a standpoint from nowhere in particular, and so makes its claims harder to locate and therefore harder to contest. Its objectivity is sometimes real, but it is always also a manner, and a manner can be adopted by writers whose claims have not earned it. None of this licenses formlessness. Provisionality is easily counterfeited, and the meandering essay that circles its subject without ever risking a claim is as familiar as the rigid one, and less useful. A thought cannot be tested unless it is first stated with enough definiteness to fail. A genuine attempt is one that might not succeed, and an essay that cannot fail because it never claims anything has not attempted anything at all. The essay at its best is therefore not the opposite of argument but argument conducted in the open, where the reader can see each step taken and judge for herself whether it holds.
R07-A-08: Many of the long novels of the nineteenth century first reached their readers not as books but in instalments, issued monthly or weekly over a year or more, in magazines or in separate parts. Modern criticism has tended to treat this fact as an extenuating circumstance. When such a novel sprawls, introduces a character it later forgets, or closes a chapter on a contrived moment of suspense, the serial is invoked as an excuse: the author was writing to deadline, paid by length, obliged to bring readers back next month. The implication is that the real novel, the one the author would have written in better conditions, lies somewhere beneath the one we have, and that serial publication is a kind of noise to be filtered out. The trouble with this view is that it treats the serial only as a set of pressures, when it was also a set of possibilities, and many of the qualities we now admire in these books grew from it. A novel read over eighteen months is lived with in a way that a novel read over a week is not. Its characters age alongside their readers; its crises arrive amid the readers' own. The large casts and interwoven plots that later critics found unwieldy were in part a response to this rhythm, since a reader returning after a month's absence needed several lines of interest to pick up, and recurring figures with distinctive habits of speech helped her find her place. What looks in a single volume like digression could, at the pace of first reading, serve as the texture of a world one returned to. Serial publication also made the novel unusually public while it was still unfinished. An instalment could be discussed before the next was written, and authors could, and sometimes did, adjust their plans in light of how readers responded. A purist may regard this as a surrender of artistic control. It can as easily be seen as a kind of conversation, in which a book took shape partly through its encounter with an audience rather than being delivered complete to readers whose only role was to receive it. For a time the novel became a shared event, followed by readers who knew that a great many others were reading the same pages in the same weeks. None of this is to deny the costs. Writing to fixed lengths did produce padding, and the demand for suspense at the end of each part did produce cliffhangers that the story did not need and that read awkwardly once the parts were bound together. A reader of the collected volume is entitled to notice these. What deserves suspicion is the standard against which they are judged as failures: the ideal of the novel as a single, unified design, conceived whole and executed according to plan. That ideal has a history of its own, and it gained much of its authority later, among writers and critics who worked for a different market and under different conditions. Applied backward, it does not so much reveal the faults of serial fiction as convert its differences into faults. There is, finally, an irony in the critical embarrassment. Long television dramas, released in episodes and discussed between them, are now often praised by critics for the very qualities, the slow accumulation, the large cast, the sense of a world lived alongside, that the instalment novel was once thought to need excusing for. Nothing about the newer form proves the older one right, and a slack episode is no better for belonging to a celebrated series. But the shift in judgement suggests that what critics of the instalment novel took for timeless standards of form were, at least in part, the habits of one particular way of reading.
